'''Julius Wolff''' (18 April 1882 &ndash; 8 February 1945)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.joodsmonument.nl/person/446320/en |title=Joods Monument - Julius Wolff |access-date=21 October 2012 |archive-date=25 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925110826/http://www.joodsmonument.nl/person/446320/en |url-status=dead }}</ref> was a [[Dutch people|Dutch]]-[[Jewish]] [[mathematician]], known for the [[Denjoy–Wolff theorem]] and for his boundary version of the [[Schwarz lemma]].{{#tag:ref|{{cite journal | author=J. A. Barrau | title=In Memoriam Prof. Dr. J. Wolff | journal=[[Nieuw Archief voor Wiskunde]] | volume=2 | number=22 | pages=113–114 | year=1947 | url=http://resolver.kb.nl/resolve?urn=MMKWG01:022164001:00001 }} with portrait<ref name="Alberts.2003">quoted from Gerard Alberts, Amsterdam, blog post of [http://mathforum.org/kb/message.jspa?messageID=1184925 Feb. 3, 2003] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310074107/http://mathforum.org/kb/message.jspa?messageID=1184925 |date=10 March 2018 }} at mathforum.org</ref>}}{{#tag:ref|{{cite book | contribution=Wiskunde | author=J. G. van der Corput| pages=255&mdash;291 (263&mdash;299 in the pdf file)| editor=Karel Frederik Proost and Jan Romein | title=Geestelijk Nederland 1920-1940 | location=Amsterdam | publisher=Kosmos | volume=II | year=1948 |url=http://www.dbnl.org/arch/proo002gees02_01/pag/proo002gees02_01.pdf }} This article has a separate one-page-section on the importance of J. Wolff (p.279-280 in the pdf file), and a portrait (p.275).<ref name="Alberts.2003"/>}}<ref name="van Maanen">{{Cite web |url=http://www.fisme.science.uu.nl/staff/janm/docs/portret_Julius_Wolff-totaal-20180129.pdf |title=(J.A. van Maanen:) Julius Wolff (1882-1945) (Biography in Dutch) |access-date=9 March 2018 |archive-date=10 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310010357/http://www.fisme.science.uu.nl/staff/janm/docs/portret_Julius_Wolff-totaal-20180129.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> With his family he was arrested in Utrecht by the [[Netherlands in World War II|Nazi occupation forces of the Netherlands]] on 8 March 1943 and transported to the [[Bergen-Belsen concentration camp]] on 13 September 1944, where he died of [[epidemic typhus]] on 8 February 1945, shortly before the camp was liberated.<ref name="van Maanen" /><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.ushmm.org/online/hsv/source_view.php?SourceId=25721 | title=Holocaust Survivors and Victims Database -- Registry of Names of the Bergen-Belsen Concentration Camp Prisoners }}</ref>

Wolff studied mathematics and physics at the [[University of Amsterdam]], where he earned his doctorate in 1908 under [[Diederik Korteweg|Korteweg]] with thesis ''Dynamen, beschouwd als duale vectoren''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=74732|name=Julius Wolff}}</ref> From 1907 to 1917 he taught at secondary and grammar schools in [[Meppel]], [[Middelburg, Zeeland|Middelburg]], and [[Amsterdam]]. In 1917 Wolff was appointed [[Professor]] of differential calculus,  theory of functions and higher algebra at the [[University of Groningen]] and in 1922 at [[Utrecht University]]. He was also a statistical advisor for the life insurance company (or co-operative distributive society) "Eigen Hulp," (a predecessor of [[Aegon N.V.|AEGON]]) with offices at [[The Hague]].<ref>[http://www.joodsmonument.nl/page/446318/en Joods Monument - Julius Wolff and his family]</ref>
